Alfalfa is a plant grown primarily to feed animals, but it also has uses in human food and health.

Alfalfa is a flowering plant — a short, bushy, upright plant that typically grows about 30 to 90 centimetres (1 to 3 feet) tall. It has small leaves arranged in sets of three, much like clover, and produces small purple or violet flowers. It belongs to the legume family, which is the same family as peas, beans, and lentils.

It is a perennial plant, meaning once you plant it, it keeps growing back season after season without needing to be replanted. And unusually, it can be harvested several times in a single year — sometimes 4 to 12 times depending on the climate.

One of its most remarkable physical features is its root system. Alfalfa roots can go extremely deep into the ground — sometimes 4 to 6 metres (15 to 20 feet) deep. This allows it to draw water and nutrients from deep in the earth, which makes it highly drought-resistant and extraordinarily nutritious.

Alfalfa is grown all over the world. It thrives in temperate climates with plenty of sunlight. Countries like the United States, China, Argentina, and Australia are among the biggest producers. In British English and in many countries outside North America, alfalfa is commonly called lucerne — so if you ever see that word, it refers to the exact same plant.

1. Animal feed — its primary use

The biggest and most important use of alfalfa is as feed for livestock. Cattle (especially dairy cows), horses, sheep, goats, and rabbits eat it in large quantities. It is considered one of the most valuable forage crops in the world because it is extremely rich in protein, calcium, and other essential nutrients. Animals fed on alfalfa tend to be healthy and productive.

Farmers typically dry alfalfa and compress it into rectangular blocks called alfalfa hay or alfalfa bales. These are easy to store and transport, and you will often see them stacked on farms. You can also find alfalfa sold as alfalfa pellets, a compressed form used in pet food for rabbits, guinea pigs, chinchillas, and similar animals.

2. Alfalfa sprouts — for human eating

When alfalfa seeds are soaked in water and allowed to germinate (begin growing), they produce thin, delicate white shoots with tiny pale green leaves at the tip. These are called alfalfa sprouts. They are mild in flavour, slightly crunchy, and are commonly eaten raw in salads, sandwiches, and wraps. They are rich in vitamins and are popular in health-conscious cooking.

3. Health supplements

Alfalfa is sold in the form of tablets, capsules, and powder as a dietary supplement. People take it for its high content of vitamins A, C, E, and K, as well as minerals like calcium, potassium, and iron. It is sometimes brewed as a herbal tea as well.

4. Improving the soil

Alfalfa has a special biological ability: like other legumes, it can take nitrogen gas from the air and, with the help of bacteria that live in nodules on its roots, convert it into a form that enriches the soil. This process is called nitrogen fixation. Because of this, farmers often grow alfalfa to naturally improve the fertility of their fields before planting other crops. It acts as a kind of natural fertilizer for the soil.

Alfalfa is sometimes called the "Queen of Forages" in agricultural circles, and for good reason. The global dairy and livestock industry depends heavily on it. Without alfalfa as a reliable, nutritious, high-yield feed crop, producing the milk, cheese, butter, and meat that billions of people consume would be far more difficult and expensive.

Beyond farming, it quietly shows up in health food stores, salad bars, and kitchen gardens around the world. It is one of those plants that most people encounter without realizing it — whether in a bowl of sprouts, in a supplement capsule, or in a bale of hay on a farm.
Quick summary of the forms you'll encounter

• Alfalfa (the plant itself, growing in a field)
  • Alfalfa hay (dried alfalfa, fed to large animals like cows and horses)
  • Alfalfa pellets (compressed feed, mainly for small animals like rabbits)
  • Alfalfa sprouts (germinated seeds, eaten by humans)
  • Alfalfa supplements (tablets or powder, taken for nutrition)
  • Lucerne (the same plant, called by this name in British English and many other countries)
